title: Occupy the place the mind already has available.
dek: Ries and Trout begin positioning with a ruthless correction: communication does not happen in the market you wish existed. It happens inside an overloaded prospect's existing mind.

marginNote.label: Apprenticeship Note
marginNote.body: Do not start with what the product wants to say. Start with what the prospect already believes, remembers, compares, ignores, and has room to accept.

canon.heading: Ries and Trout: Positioning begins in the prospect's mind.
canon.standfirst: Read Chapter 1, "What Positioning Is All About," from Al Ries and Jack Trout's Positioning. The chapter establishes the outside-in premise: the winning move is not to invent a reality, but to work with the mental structures already present.
canon.readerIntro: Read this short chapter slowly. It is not a toolkit yet; it is a correction of instinct. Watch how Ries and Trout move from creativity and communication toward reality, mental overload, simplification, and the prospect's point of view.

blocks.label: 01 / Start with reality, not invention
paragraphs: Ries and Trout open by puncturing a common creative fantasy: in an overcrowded market, the marketer does not get a blank mental canvas. The only reality that matters is the one already lodged in the prospect's mind.
As you read, mark every place they redirect attention away from the product and toward the prospect. That move is the foundation of positioning.

blocks.label: 02 / Notice the constraint on communication
paragraphs: The chapter treats the mind as defensive. Because people receive too much information, they screen, reject, and simplify. More communication does not automatically create more meaning.
Do not read this as pessimism. Read it as design discipline: if the mind is selective, the message must fit a slot the prospect can actually use.

blocks.label: 03 / Study oversimplification
paragraphs: Ries and Trout's answer is not to make the product smaller. It is to make the message sharper. The burden is on the communicator to strip away ambiguity until one position can enter the mind.
This is where good taste becomes commercial leverage: not ornament, not cleverness, but the courage to make one idea unmistakable.

blocks.label: 04 / Turn the process around
paragraphs: The closing movement is the practical heart of the chapter: focus on the prospect rather than the product. The communicator is not the judge of clarity; the receiver is.
Use the chapter to build an outside-in habit. Before writing a claim, ask what mental comparison the prospect is already making and what existing belief your message can retie.

focusing on the prospect rather than the product
closeReading: Write Ries and Trout's definition of positioning in your own words. What does it shift away from the product and toward the prospect?
List three things your audience already believes about your category before you say a word.
Find the chapter's argument for why more communication can reduce actual communication. Where do you see this in current brand behavior?
Choose one product you care about. What position is already occupied in the prospect's mind, and what position is realistically still available?
Reduce one messy product claim to a single outside-in sentence a prospect could remember.

principle.heading: A position is accepted when it fits the mind's existing map.
principle.body: Positioning is not self-expression by a brand. It is disciplined selection: choose the simplest, most credible place you can occupy in a prospect's already crowded mind.
principle.example: A project-management app can say it is "AI-powered work orchestration," but the prospect may only have room for "the thing that keeps client work from slipping." The second phrase has a mental slot.
principle.practice: Pick one offer. Write the category ladder your prospect already has in their head, including the default choice, the premium choice, the cheap choice, and the confusing alternatives. Then write one position you can credibly own without asking them to rebuild the ladder.

signals.heading: Three reminders that the available position is set by the customer's actual environment.

fieldNotes.title: AI search exposes the digital estate a brand has already left behind
fieldNotes.whatHappened: A TechRadar Pro analysis argues that brands are increasingly represented in AI answers by the scattered material already available online, including outdated pages and contradictory documents; its cited assessment found only a small share of major brand sites leading on AI readiness.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Ries and Trout's outside-in premise now has a technical corollary: the market's mental map is partly assembled from the public evidence a brand has already made easy to retrieve. A new claim cannot reliably outrun stale proof.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether teams give one owner the job of reconciling product facts, policies, and legacy pages before optimizing their phrasing for AI discovery.

fieldNotes.title: The agent pitch shifts from making assets to running a defined business job
fieldNotes.whatHappened: In an interview, Bluehost's CEO distinguishes single-asset AI tools from agents intended to carry a bounded business outcome across workflows, such as a front desk that answers questions, checks availability, and books appointments from current business information.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: Positioning improves when the category is named by the job a customer can recognize. 'An AI agent' is abstract; a reliably bounded role gives the prospect a usable comparison and a reason to believe it.
fieldNotes.watch: Whether vendors limit early agents to narrow, inspectable permissions rather than asking customers to accept an expansive autonomous promise.

fieldNotes.title: Social channels remain part of the route into consumer technology purchases
fieldNotes.whatHappened: CivicScience's recent Q3 consumer-electronics shopping-intent analysis points to social media as an increasingly important influence on tech buying across age groups, alongside a high-intent segment planning a purchase within three months.
fieldNotes.whyItMatters: A position is not merely a sentence on a landing page; it must survive in the channels where a category is compared. The message needs a compact, recognizable slot before the buyer reaches the product page.
fieldNotes.watch: Which technology brands preserve the same category cue from social discovery through comparison and purchase rather than changing the promise at each step.

signals.tweetHeading: Two fragments on the position a product earns by solving a visible job.

tweets.author: Ben Zhang
tweets.title: A one-off tool earns clarity from the moment of need
tweets.summary: Zhang's account of using an AI-generated Bluetooth meter to find a lost phone is a useful positioning test: the value becomes legible as a concrete job completed, not as a general claim about AI capability.
tweets.text: Lost my phone at the office and spent 30 minutes turning the place over. Find My was disabled by MDM. Out of ideas, I asked Claude how I could find it. It suggested tracking the Bluetooth signal strength, then wrote me a meter in about a minute. I walked around watching the number climb. Found it. Apparently you can just make the tool you need now.

tweets.author: signüll
tweets.title: A visible substitute changes the default comparison
tweets.summary: This Waymo anecdote makes a category shift unusually concrete: the comparison is no longer an autonomous-car future but the total cost and friction of a teenager's car. That is the mental ladder the service must win.
tweets.text: i met someone who waymos her daughter to school & back everyday. they calculated the cost for a car, gas, & insurance for a 16 year old driver is more expensive than using waymo’s. the future is remarkably visible but not yet full accessible.

output.heading: Draw one ladder in the mind.
output.body: After reading, choose a real category and sketch the prospect's mental ladder before you write any message. The useful output is not a clever line; it is the available position the line must serve.
